Research/MGA
Feedback-informed interaction

MGA
Refine interaction through its physical response.

In contact, a displacement command can produce motion, deformation, force, or a jam. Manifold Generative Annealing combines learned interaction proposals with model-based evaluation and feedback-conditioned geometric refinement. It jointly optimizes short motion–impedance sequences, then replans as contact evolves. Learned experience supplies candidate behaviors; the generative optimizer does not require a learned denoising score.

Figures & tablesRun this method

The question

How can learned interaction strategies be reassessed and corrected when current contact conditions differ from training or nominal predictions?

Demonstrations

How it works

01

Propose useful behaviors

Pretrained RL policies generate structured short-horizon proposals alongside Gaussian exploration. Depending on the integration mode, learned horizons join the refinement bank or compete separately at execution selection.

02

Reassess with dynamics

Common closed-loop model rollouts evaluate candidates under current conditions. Rollout weighting forms an update without a learned density or score; a favorable candidate is not automatically committed to execution.

03

Refine for realization

Where enabled, tracking and contact feedback adjust the task references used to define local residuals. Geometry shapes the update, and response reliability modulates refinement strength.

04

Correct residuals and replan

Local Residual Correction (LRC) applies a damped Jacobian step to residuals left after directional shaping and finite updates. The controller executes the first primitive and shifts the remaining horizon for the next solve.

Results

The paper studies executed contact-rich behavior across surface scanning, peg insertion, and fixed-stance humanoid interaction. The original results retain both successful and failed conditions, separate safe completion from raw completion, and evaluate the learned proposal prior through controlled simulation ablations.

Experimental protocol and metric definitions

S uses task-specific safe-success criteria. Scanning requires at least 90% contact-valid coverage within 5 mm, at most 10% settled contact loss, and permits at most one of 100 force samples to exceed 60 N.

Peg-insertion safe success requires a complete 64-step execution without any wrench violation or jam, including after first completion. ID is nominal; Pose-OOD perturbs socket pose; Sensing-OOD biases wrench observations. Safety uses true simulated loads.

F is dimensionless normalized load-tail risk. Scanning and humanoid force are normalized by a 60 N limit; peg insertion uses the maximum normalized axial/lateral force and bending/torsional torque utilization. Lower loads alone do not imply completion.

† and ‡: Unjamming tails without the prior and without LRC are conditional on eight and three accepted runs, respectively; rejected prefixes count as failures. These tails are not ranked against the ten-run MGA estimate.

The prior is evaluated additively in peg insertion and the reported humanoid runs: one deterministic and eight stochastic learned horizons compete with the refined Gaussian sequence. This is not an equal-total-rollout-cost comparison with the no-prior ablation.

Humanoid results cover 15 N force regulation, a nominal 8 kg box pushed 0.10 m from fixed stance, and 0.03 m unjamming with yaw correction. Walking pushes and randomized pushing conditions are not in this comparison.

These are results of the paper protocol, separate from V1 GPU qualification and robot-controller deployment support.

Experimental protocol and metric definitions

All 15 scans reach their path endpoint. Complete-session outcomes are 5/5 for table, 4/5 for foam, and 5/5 for phantom; one foam session stops because robot feedback becomes stale after scanning and release.

The force calibration has a held-out 95th-percentile residual of 1.14 N. These metrics characterize compensated feedback rather than independently verified absolute contact force.

The hardware protocol uses a 0.4 s horizon, 48 candidate sequences, nominal 10 Hz planning and 20 Hz position commands, with bounded normal-force feedback. Results reflect the planner and feedback controller together.

Scope & trade-offs

Simulation covers surface scanning, peg insertion, and Unitree H1 pushing. Dobot Nova 5 hardware demonstrations evaluate the model-based component without an RL proposal prior, using position commands with force feedback. They do not directly execute a full Cartesian stiffness matrix.

LRC is a local correction, not an exact projection or hard-feasibility guarantee. Unseen-surface safe success is 50%; the 100% results for nominal hard, soft, and hybrid groups should not be generalized to unseen surfaces.

Peg and humanoid evaluations add nine learned horizons per replanning call after Gaussian refinement. These experts compete separately and do not receive that refinement. The 64-sample nominal budget does not imply equal total rollout cost.

Hardware results validate the model-based component with contact feedback, not the complete RL-assisted simulation configuration.

The next question

2GO develops geometry-aware generation for constrained locomotion. MGA extends the research direction toward contact interaction: geometric refinement is conditioned on physical response, and learned behaviors provide additional candidates. It addresses a different control setting rather than replacing 2GO's locomotion planner.

Figures and tables reproduce the manuscript's reported experiments. Demonstrations are representative runs; experimental populations and metrics are specified with each table.
